subject: science
name: Mindful Eating: A Path to a Healthy Body
summary: Food habits differ across India depending on local crops, climate and culture. Our food gives us nutrients — carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins and minerals — plus dietary fibre and water. We can test foods for starch, protein and fat. A balanced diet keeps us healthy, while a lack of certain nutrients causes deficiency diseases. Millets, local seasonal food and mindful eating habits are good choices; junk food and food waste are not.

topics.title: Food diversity across India
topics.summary: What people eat in different parts of India depends on the crops that grow there, the climate, traditions and how food habits have changed over time.
topics.simple: People in different parts of India eat different foods. In Punjab you might eat makki ki roti and sarson ka saag; in Tamil Nadu, idli and sambar; in Bengal, rice and fish. This is because different crops grow in different places, and each region has its own traditions.
topics.explain:
India has amazing **food diversity**. A thali in one state can look completely different from a thali in another.

What decides what people eat?
- **Local crops:** rice grows well in wet areas (Kerala, West Bengal, Assam), so rice is a staple there; wheat grows well in the north (Punjab, Haryana), so rotis are common
- **Climate:** people in cold regions eat more warming, energy-rich food; in hot regions, cooling foods like buttermilk (chaas) are popular
- **Coastal areas:** fish and coconut are common in coastal states like Kerala, Goa and West Bengal
- **Traditions, festivals and culture** also shape food habits

Food habits **change over time**. Our grandparents ate more millets and home-cooked local food. Today many families eat more packaged and processed foods. Asking elders about what they ate is a good way to see this change.

**Food miles** is the distance food travels from where it is grown to where it is eaten. Eating **local and seasonal** food means fewer food miles: it is fresher, often cheaper and better for the environment.
topics.example: A breakfast survey in an Indian class might find poha (Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh), aloo paratha (Punjab), idli-dosa (South India), puttu (Kerala) and luchi (Bengal). Each reflects local crops and traditions.
keyPoints: Food habits differ across regions of India
Local crops, climate and traditions shape what we eat
Rice is a staple in wet regions; wheat in the north
Food habits change over time
Food miles = distance food travels to reach us
Local, seasonal food is fresher and has fewer food miles

topics.title: Nutrients and their functions
topics.summary: Food contains nutrients: carbohydrates and fats give energy, proteins help growth and repair, vitamins and minerals protect us from disease; dietary fibre and water are also needed.
topics.simple: The useful substances in food are called **nutrients**. **Carbohydrates** and **fats** give us energy. **Proteins** help us grow and repair the body. **Vitamins** and **minerals** keep us healthy and protect us from disease. We also need **fibre** (roughage) and plenty of **water**.
topics.explain:
**Nutrients** are the components of food that our body needs. The main ones are:

- **Carbohydrates:** main source of **energy**. Found in rice, wheat, millets, potato, sugar. Starch and sugar are carbohydrates.
- **Fats:** give **more energy** than carbohydrates (for the same amount) and store energy. Found in ghee, butter, oil, nuts, milk.
- **Proteins:** needed for **growth and repair** of the body; often called body-building foods. Found in dal, pulses, milk, paneer, eggs, fish, meat, soybean.
- **Vitamins:** protect us from diseases and keep eyes, bones, teeth and gums healthy. Found in fruits, vegetables, milk. Examples: vitamin A, B, C, D.
- **Minerals:** needed in small amounts for healthy bones, teeth and blood. Examples: **calcium** (milk, ragi), **iron** (green leafy vegetables, jaggery), **iodine** (iodised salt).

Not nutrients in the same way, but just as important:
- **Dietary fibre (roughage):** helps the body get rid of undigested food and prevents constipation. Found in whole grains, fruits, vegetables, pulses with husk.
- **Water:** helps digestion, removes wastes through urine and sweat, and keeps body temperature steady.
topics.example: A meal of roti (carbohydrate), dal (protein), a little ghee (fat), palak sabzi (vitamins, iron, fibre), a glass of buttermilk (calcium, water) and a salad covers most nutrients.
keyPoints: Carbohydrates: main energy source (rice, wheat, potato)
Fats: more energy; ghee, oil, nuts
Proteins: growth and repair (dal, milk, eggs, paneer)
Vitamins: protect from disease (fruits, vegetables)
Minerals: calcium, iron, iodine — bones, blood, health
Fibre (roughage) prevents constipation; water aids digestion and removes waste

topics.title: Testing food for starch, protein and fat
topics.summary: Iodine turns starch blue-black; copper sulphate plus caustic soda turns protein violet; fat leaves an oily patch on paper.
topics.simple: We can find out what nutrients a food has with simple tests. Put a few drops of **iodine** on food: if it turns **blue-black**, there is **starch**. Rub food on paper: an **oily patch** means **fat**. Add **copper sulphate** and **caustic soda** to a food paste: a **violet** colour means **protein**.
topics.explain:
**1. Test for starch**
- Take a small piece of food (e.g. potato, rice) on a plate
- Add 2–3 drops of **dilute iodine solution**
- A **blue-black colour** shows starch is present

**2. Test for protein**
- Grind the food into a paste or powder (e.g. soaked gram, milk can be used as it is)
- Put a little in a test tube and add some water; shake
- Add **2 drops of copper sulphate solution** and **10 drops of caustic soda (sodium hydroxide) solution**
- Shake and wait a few minutes. A **violet (purple) colour** shows protein

**3. Test for fat**
- Wrap or rub the food in a piece of paper and press it
- If the paper is wet, let it dry
- An **oily (translucent) patch** that lets light through shows fat

**Safety:** Caustic soda and copper sulphate are harmful chemicals. Do these tests only with your teacher, and never taste anything in the lab.

Many foods contain more than one nutrient; for example, milk shows both protein and fat.
topics.example: Testing results you would expect: a potato slice turns blue-black with iodine (starch); a crushed peanut leaves an oily patch on paper (fat); a paste of soaked gram (chana) turns violet with copper sulphate and caustic soda (protein).
keyPoints: Starch + iodine → blue-black
Protein + copper sulphate + caustic soda → violet
Fat → oily (translucent) patch on paper
Use 2 drops copper sulphate and 10 drops caustic soda
Do chemical tests only under a teacher's supervision
One food can contain several nutrients

topics.title: Balanced diet and deficiency diseases
topics.summary: A balanced diet has all nutrients, fibre and water in the right amounts; a long-term lack of a nutrient causes deficiency diseases such as scurvy, rickets, night blindness, beriberi, goitre and anaemia.
topics.simple: A **balanced diet** gives your body all the nutrients it needs in the right amounts, plus fibre and water. If your food lacks a nutrient for a long time, you can get a **deficiency disease**. For example, too little vitamin C causes bleeding gums (scurvy), and too little iodine can cause goitre.
topics.explain:
A **balanced diet** contains carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, fibre and water in the **right amounts** for a person's needs. How much we need depends on age, whether we are male or female, how active we are and our health. A growing child, a sportsperson and an elderly person need different amounts.

Eating too little of some nutrients, or too much of others (like sugar, salt and fat), is unhealthy.

**Deficiency diseases** happen when the body does not get enough of a nutrient for a **long time**:
- **Vitamin A** → night blindness (poor vision in dim light)
- **Vitamin B1** → beriberi (weak muscles, little energy)
- **Vitamin C** → scurvy (bleeding gums, wounds heal slowly)
- **Vitamin D** → rickets (soft, bent bones in children)
- **Calcium** → weak bones and teeth
- **Iodine** → goitre (swelling in the neck)
- **Iron** → anaemia (tiredness, weakness)

Most deficiency diseases can be **prevented** by eating a balanced diet. Sunlight helps our body make vitamin D, iodised salt provides iodine, and fruits like amla, orange and lemon provide vitamin C.
topics.example: Long ago, sailors on long sea voyages often got scurvy because they ate no fresh fruit. Giving them lemons or limes prevented it — because these supply vitamin C.
keyPoints: Balanced diet = all nutrients, fibre and water in right amounts
Needs depend on age, sex, activity and health
Vitamin A → night blindness; B1 → beriberi
Vitamin C → scurvy; vitamin D → rickets
Iodine → goitre; iron → anaemia; calcium → weak bones
Deficiency diseases can be prevented by a balanced diet

topics.title: Millets, junk food and mindful eating
topics.summary: Millets are nutritious, hardy grains; junk food is high in salt, sugar and fat with few nutrients; mindful eating means eating slowly, with attention, choosing healthy food and not wasting it.
topics.simple: **Millets** like ragi, jowar and bajra are healthy grains our grandparents often ate. **Junk food** like chips, sweet drinks and fried snacks has lots of salt, sugar and fat but few nutrients. **Mindful eating** means paying attention to what and how you eat: eat slowly, without screens, stop when full, and don't waste food.
topics.explain:
**Millets** are small-grained cereals such as **ragi (finger millet), jowar (sorghum), bajra (pearl millet)**, sanwa and kodo.
- Rich in fibre, minerals (ragi is rich in **calcium**; bajra has iron) and other nutrients
- Grow with **little water** and in poor soil, so they are good for farmers and the environment
- India proposed, and the United Nations declared, **2023 as the International Year of Millets**

**Junk food** (chips, burgers, sugary drinks, many packaged snacks) usually has:
- Too much **salt, sugar and fat**
- Very little fibre, vitamins and minerals
- Eating it often can lead to unhealthy weight gain and other health problems. Read food labels to check what's inside.

**Mindful eating** means:
- Eating slowly and chewing well
- Avoiding TV or phone while eating
- Noticing hunger and stopping when full
- Enjoying the colour, smell and taste of food
- Choosing a variety of healthy, local, seasonal foods
- Taking only as much as you can eat, so **no food is wasted**
topics.example: Swapping a packet of chips for a bowl of roasted makhana or a ragi ladoo gives you fibre and minerals instead of extra salt and oil.
keyPoints: Millets: ragi, jowar, bajra — nutritious and need little water
Ragi is rich in calcium
2023 was the International Year of Millets
Junk food: high salt, sugar, fat; low nutrients
Mindful eating: eat slowly, no screens, stop when full
Don't waste food; take only what you can eat

commonMistakes: Thinking the iodine test detects protein — iodine turning blue-black shows starch.
Mixing up deficiency diseases: scurvy is vitamin C, rickets is vitamin D, goitre is iodine, anaemia is iron.
Thinking fibre is useless because it isn't digested — it helps the body remove undigested food.
Thinking a balanced diet means eating equal amounts of every food — it means the right amount of each nutrient.
Forgetting water as an essential part of the diet.
Thinking millets are 'poor' food — they are highly nutritious.

faqs.q: Which nutrient gives us the most energy?
faqs.a: **Fats** give the most energy for the same amount of food, but **carbohydrates** are our main everyday source of energy because we eat them in larger amounts (rice, roti, millets).

faqs.q: How do I test a food for starch, protein and fat?
faqs.a:
- **Starch:** add dilute iodine → blue-black colour
- **Protein:** food paste + water + 2 drops copper sulphate + 10 drops caustic soda → violet colour
- **Fat:** rub on paper → oily, translucent patch

Do the chemical tests only with your teacher.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a balanced diet and a healthy-looking meal?
faqs.a: A meal can look full and tasty but still miss nutrients. A **balanced diet** is about having all the nutrients, fibre and water in the right amounts. For example, a plate of only fried snacks is filling but lacks proteins, vitamins and fibre.

Millets like ragi, jowar and bajra are rich in fibre and minerals (ragi has a lot of calcium). They also grow with little water and in poor soil, so they are healthy for us and good for farmers and the environment.
**Food miles** is the distance food travels from the farm to your plate. Food grown nearby and in season travels less, so it's fresher and uses less fuel for transport.

quiz.q: Which nutrient is mainly needed for growth and repair of the body?
A food turns blue-black when iodine is added. It contains:
In the protein test, which two solutions are added?
quiz.explain: 2 drops of copper sulphate and 10 drops of caustic soda give a violet colour if protein is present.

quiz.q: A crushed peanut leaves a translucent patch on paper. This shows the presence of:
quiz.explain: An oily, translucent patch shows fat.

quiz.q: Bleeding gums and slow healing of wounds are signs of:
quiz.explain: Scurvy is caused by a lack of vitamin C.

quiz.q: Lack of iodine in the diet can cause:
quiz.explain: Iodine deficiency can cause goitre (swelling in the neck). Iodised salt helps prevent it.

quiz.q: Rickets, which makes bones soft and bent in children, is caused by lack of:
quiz.explain: Vitamin D (along with calcium) is needed for strong bones.

options: Helps remove undigested food and prevents constipation
quiz.explain: Fibre isn't digested but helps the body get rid of undigested food.

quiz.q: Which of these is a millet rich in calcium?
quiz.explain: Ragi (finger millet) is known for its high calcium content.

quiz.q: Which is an example of mindful eating?
options: Eating slowly and stopping when full
Taking more food than you can finish
quiz.explain: Mindful eating means paying attention, eating slowly and not overeating or wasting food.

How far you walk after eating
The distance food travels from where it is grown to where it is eaten

quiz.q: Rice is a staple food in Kerala, West Bengal and Assam mainly because:
options: It is the cheapest food in the world
It is imported from other countries
Rice grows well in these wet regions
quiz.explain: Local crops shape food habits; rice needs plenty of water, which these regions have.
